newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss leave door open for boosting Holocaust fund.
newsitem.headline: Swiss leave door open for boosting Holocaust fund.

text.p: The Swiss government may boost its proposed Holocaust memorial fund in a gesture of good will demanded by world Jewish organisations, an authoritative Berne political source said on Wednesday.

A Swiss cabinet statement on Tuesday deliberately left open a door for adding government money to a planned fund drawing on some 40 million Swiss francs ($30 million) in dormant Swiss bank accounts, the source close to the issue said.

Jewish leaders, who have pressed Berne to make restitution for alleged Swiss profiteering from the Holocaust, had slammed the cabinet proposal for using other people's abandoned bank accounts rather than Swiss public funds.

But the Federal Council, or cabinet, included wording in its statement allowing a quick pay out of federal funds if Berne's ongoing research confirms charges of Swiss wrongdoing towards Jews and others Nazi victims, the source told Reuters.
"This sentence doesn't mean much to most people, but this is a very important sentence," said the source, who declined to be named.
The sentence in question reads:
"Should substantiated facts be found which require immediate action, even while the investigation process is under way, the Federal Council will immediately take the necessary steps.
"This also applies to different demands regarding damage payments which have recently become ever more vocal," the official statement added.

Groups led by the World Jewish Congress (WJC) have suggested the Swiss make a good faith financial gesture soon, before a report due in two to five years from historians probing Swiss financial dealings with Jews and Nazis during World War Two.
The Berne source said this point would be stressed in talks with Jewish leaders, who last week threatened to call a boycott of Swiss banks to vent their displeasure.

The cabinet's wording meant it could decide on Holocaust payments even before interim reports from the panel of nine Swiss and foreign historians commissioned by the Swiss government last month, the source added.
For example, the cabinet could act based on new conclusions about its war-time refugee policy.

Switzerland last year gave one million Swiss francs to the Auschwitz memorial and a counselling group for Holocaust survivors in a gesture of reconciliation after apologising for a wartime policy of turning back Jewish refugees from Nazi terror.

Jewish officials note that another aspect of Berne's wartime policy was a requirement that Jewish groups support Jewish refugees allowed into the country during the Holocaust, while the government paid for all other war refugees.
Swiss and foreign Jewish groups spent about 55 million Swiss francs in 1940s prices for their refugees, the Swiss Jewish Federation says.

Separately, Berne's special ambassador on Jewish accounts and wartime financial deals, Thomas Borer, denied that he had put forward the figure of $250 million in talks late last year on a possible Swiss payment.

A Jewish source close to the talks said in New York that Berne had been receptive to a Jewish proposal for a financial gesture to Holocaust victims and that a Swiss representative had proposed the $250 million number.
The source spoke on Tuesday to rebut a charge by former Swiss President and current Economics Minister Jean-Pascal Delamuraz that the request was "extortion and blackmail".
The Swiss government refused to rebuke Delamuraz on Tuesday, despite warnings that the World Jewish Restitution Organisation might call for a boycott of Swiss banks if it did not.

Borer said he would contact Jewish groups soon to try to ease tension over Berne's failure to condemn Delamuraz, who has said he regretted any offence his remarks caused but did not withdraw them. ($1=1.3584 Swiss Franc)
